topic: Structure of the Modern Periodic Table
title: Why 18 Columns? The Table Explained Simply | PUC Chemistry Class 11
description:
On a calendar every Sunday sits in one column, and in a cinema you find your seat by row and number. Rows and columns turn a crowd into an address, and the periodic table works the same way. In this animated lesson for PUC and Class 11 Chemistry (NCERT Chapter 3, Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties) we see why the modern table has the shape it has.

You will see the long form light up: 7 periods (rows), 18 groups (columns, numbered 1 to 18 by IUPAC in place of the old IA to VIIB labels), and the lanthanoids and actinoids in two rows at the bottom. On the molecule bench, electrons fill the orbitals of each period one by one, and every electron added is one more element: 2 in period 1, 8 in periods 2 and 3, and 18 in period 4 when the 3d orbitals join. A worked example counts the 16 orbitals of period 6 to get 32 elements, then the 2n squared exam trap, an original JEE Main pattern question with a full solution, a recap card and three questions to check yourself.

This is Episode 28 of our PUC Chemistry series.

Made for PUC (Karnataka), CBSE Class 11, NEET and JEE Main students.

In this video:
0:00 Rows and columns make an address
0:34 The long form: 7 periods, 18 groups
1:02 What a group and a period share
1:11 Why periods have different lengths
1:56 Period 4 and the d orbitals
2:13 Group vs period + pause and think
2:43 Worked example: period 6 has 32 elements
3:15 Exam trap: 2n squared is not the period length
3:38 Practice question (JEE Main pattern)
4:16 Recap and three questions to answer
